title: Joining the sangat
hook: the code encourages visiting the gurdwara and learning Gurbani together

segments.voice: Yesterday, rising early: get up, wash, and give the first word of the day to the Name. Your line was rise and remember. What did your day hear first this morning? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

Why does a song you've hummed alone in the car sound different in a room full of people singing it? Alone, you skip the lines you don't know. In the room, someone beside you knows them, and you lean on their voice until you've got it. Somebody hits the high note you were afraid of. Somebody else keeps time. By the end you know the song better than you did, and you can't say exactly who taught you. The Sikh code has a word for that room, and it asks a Sikh not to stay home in the car.
screen: `ALONE IN THE CAR.` → `A ROOM FULL OF VOICES.` → `YOU CAN'T SAY WHO TAUGHT YOU.`

segments.voice: The word is sangat: company, the gathered congregation. In paraphrase, the code says that the Guru's word sinks in more readily and more deeply when a Sikh hears it in the sangat, and so it encourages Sikhs to visit the gurdwara and join the congregation there, to listen, and to reflect on Gurbani together. Notice what the code is claiming. Not that the gurdwara is the only place the word can be heard. A Sikh has nitnem at home, morning and night. The claim is about depth. Some things you take in better with others in the room. Now, which room? Guru Nanak asks that question himself, in Siri Rag. In paraphrase: how is the true company known? Where the One Name alone is spoken of. That's the test. Not the size of the hall. Not who built it or who's in charge. A sangat is known by what is said there. So a crowded hall with something else at its center would fail the test, and a few people at a kitchen table reading Gurbani together would pass it. And look at the verbs in the code: hear, reflect, learn. This isn't only about showing up. In a sangat one person catches a line another missed. Someone explains a word. A child picks up a melody before she can read it. A newcomer hears a hymn for the first time in the voices of people who've loved it for years. The learning moves sideways, from person to person, not only from the front. That's today's line. Not learn alone, then gather. Learn together.
screen: `SANGAT: THE GATHERED COMPANY.` · `THE WORD SINKS IN MORE DEEPLY.` · `KNOWN BY WHAT IS SAID THERE.` · `LEARNING MOVES SIDEWAYS.` · then, large: `LEARN TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go, or plan to go. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a gathering where something good is learned together: a gurdwara, a study group, a class, a table where people read aloud. Gurdwaras are open to visitors from any background. Now make it concrete. Which day could you go? Who could you go with? What would make you stay a little longer than you planned? If you can't go anywhere this week, choose one person to read or listen with. Then rest until the bell, holding that plan. The bell holds the time.
Joining the sangat. Going to the gathered company, where the code says the Guru's word sinks in more deeply, and where Guru Nanak says the true company is known by the Name. Today's word.
Your line: learn together. Today, learn one thing from someone beside you rather than from a screen, and tell them it landed. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs gather in the gurdwara to hear kirtan, listen to explanations of Gurbani and join the Ardas; families often go together, and gurdwaras welcome visitors.

fork.reveal: the code encourages joining the sangat in the gurdwara, to hear and reflect together, because the word sinks in more deeply there.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sangat is just the crowd at a gurdwara.
what it means: the gathered company where, the code says, the Guru's word sinks in more deeply.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak defines the true company by what is said there, the One Name, not by its place (Ang 72).
